1732-1809; 'father of the symphony and string quartet'; 104 symphonies.
1770-1827; bridged Classical and Romantic; 9 symphonies including the 5th and 9th ('Choral').
Three-part structure: exposition, development, recapitulation; basis of first movements.

Strophic storytelling song passed down the oral tradition, with the same melody repeated for each verse of the story.
Brazilian carnival music driven by layered percussion such as the large surdo drums, built on interlocking syncopated patterns.
Instruments typical of British and Irish folk music, including fiddle, tin whistle, accordion and the bodhran frame drum.
Accenting off-beats or weak beats against a steady pulse, a defining rhythmic feature of Caribbean, Latin American and African styles.

Intense early twentieth-century style using extreme dissonance, angular melody and dramatic contrasts to express inner emotion.

Style built from short repeated patterns that change gradually, associated with Steve Reich and Philip Glass from the 1960s onwards.
Twentieth-century movement reviving the clear forms and textures of the eighteenth century with modern harmony, associated with Stravinsky.
Composers since 1910 expanded sound with note clusters, extended playing techniques and a much larger role for percussion.

area-of-study-1-western-classical-music-.d: Area of Study 1: Western Classical Music 1600-1910
terms: Roughly 1600-1750: ornamented melodies over a basso continuo, terraced dynamics and counterpoint; key figures include Bach, Handel and Vivaldi.
Baroque accompaniment of a bass line played by cello or bassoon with chords filled in on harpsichord or organ.
Roughly 1750-1820: balanced phrases, clear textures and sonata form, perfected by Haydn, Mozart and the young Beethoven.
Instrumental music that depicts a story, scene or idea, a favourite Romantic genre exemplified by the symphonic poem.
Roughly 1810-1910: expanded orchestras, richer chromatic harmony and extremes of expression, with composers such as Brahms and Tchaikovsky.
Three-part design of exposition, development and recapitulation that underpins most first movements of Classical symphonies and sonatas.
Music heard by characters in the film world (e.g., a radio playing).
German composer; The Lion King, Inception, Dune; pioneer of orchestral-electronic hybrid.
American composer; Star Wars, Jaws, Harry Potter, ET themes.
Recurring theme for a character; used extensively in film since Wagner.
Music for the audience only, not heard by characters; the conventional film score.
Continuous background music that accompanies film action without dialogue.

area-of-study-3-musical-traditions-of-ir.d: Area of Study 3: Musical Traditions of Ireland
terms: 1678-1741; Italian composer of 'The Four Seasons' violin concertos.
Music from ~1600-1750; ornate, contrapuntal, with continuo bass line.
Continuous bass line played by cello/harpsichord, supporting Baroque ensembles.
Polyphonic form with a subject introduced and developed in multiple voices.
1685-1750; master of counterpoint, wrote 'The Well-Tempered Clavier' and Brandenburg Concertos.

terms: Pitch-correction software used subtly to fix vocal tuning, or pushed hard as a deliberate robotic vocal effect.
Modern records are built in digital audio workstation software, where parts are recorded, edited, quantised and mixed on screen.
Device for programming drum patterns, whose punchy electronic beats underpinned 1980s pop, hip-hop and electronic dance music.
Promotional film for a song; after MTV launched in 1981, striking visuals became central to how pop reached its audience.
Reusing an extract of an existing recording within a new track, a foundation of hip-hop and dance music from the 1980s onwards.
Electronic instrument that generates and shapes sounds, defining the synth-pop of the 1980s and much dance and pop production since.

area-of-study-3-music-for-stage-and-scre.d: Area of Study 3: Music for Stage and Screen
terms: Climactic number ending a musical's first act; 'Defying Gravity' closes Act One of 'Wicked' on a dramatic high point.
Diegetic music is heard by the characters within the story; non-diegetic music, like most underscore, is heard only by the audience.
Bold brass flourish; the Star Wars Main Title opens with a triumphant trumpet fanfare that instantly establishes the heroic mood.
Recurring theme linked to a character or idea; John Williams binds the Star Wars films together with leitmotifs introduced in the Main Title.
Music running beneath dialogue and action to support mood and pacing without drawing attention away from the drama.
Music illustrating the meaning of the lyrics, such as rising melodic lines matching images of flight in 'Defying Gravity' from 'Wicked'.
Esperanza Spalding's jazz performance of a Brazilian bossa nova song, featuring her voice with double bass and acoustic guitar.
Group whose track 'Release' fuses Irish Celtic folk, West African music and electronic dance production in layered grooves.
Gentle syncopated Brazilian groove derived from samba, supporting lyrical melody in an intimate, quiet texture.
Music that blends features of different traditions - rhythms, instruments, scales and production - into a coherent new style.
West African instruments heard in Afro Celt music: the kora is a 21-string harp-lute, the talking drum bends pitch under the arm.
Fusion producers combine loops, drones and live instruments in the studio, building textures gradually across a track.

terms: Three crotchet beats per bar; used for waltzes.
Four crotchet beats per bar; the most common signature in popular music.
Six quaver beats grouped in twos; a swaying, dance-like feel.
Two numbers at the start of a piece: top = beats per bar, bottom = note value of beat.

Combining elements from different musical traditions, as in Paul Simon's 'Graceland' (1986) with South African mbaqanga.

Use of intervals smaller than a semitone, characteristic of Arabic maqam and Indian raga systems.
Music passed down by listening and imitation rather than notation, the primary transmission mode for most world musics.
Simultaneous combination of contrasting rhythms, particularly developed in sub-Saharan African drumming.

Short, catchy melodic or lyrical idea crafted to stick in the memory, usually placed in the chorus and often in the title line.
Slow, emotional song that builds from an intimate opening to a big climactic final chorus, prominent from the 1970s to the 1990s.
1950s style built on the 12-bar blues progression with energetic vocals, backbeat drumming and prominent electric guitar.
1970s-80s stadium style with powerful guitar riffs, big singalong choruses and extended guitar solos.
Pop's standard plan of verses telling the story and a repeated chorus carrying the hook, often with an intro, bridge and outro.
